title: In vivo optical recordings of ion dynamics in mouse corneal primary nociceptive terminals
protocol: Sterilize the surgical tools using the glass bead dry sterilizer.
Anesthetize a 4-6 weeks old adult male mouse by intraperitoneal injection of 100 μL of anesthesia mixture.
Shave the top of the mouse scalp.
Place the mouse in the stereotactic frame on a heating pad set at 37°C.
Attach the teeth to the mouthpiece.
Assemble the nose cone connected to the isoflurane vaporizer.
Set vaporizer to 2% for anesthesia induction.
Set the oxygen flow rate in the vaporizer to 350–400 mL/min.
Apply eye ointment to both eyes to avoid dryness.
Monitor pain reflexes by observing responses to paw pinching.
Decrease isoflurane percentage to 0.4%–0.6% for anesthesia maintenance once reflexes are diminished.
Visually monitor the breathing rate during the entire procedure.
Stabilize and fix the head in the stereotactic frame using non-rupture ear bars.
Inject meloxicam subcutaneously (SC) for pain relief at a concentration of 1.32–1.65 mg/kg.
Use hair removal cream for removing the remaining fur after shaving.
Clean and sterilize the scalp with alternating swabs of 70% ethanol and 10% povidone iodine.
Dry the area.
Make a 1 cm midline incision to expose the Bregma and Lambda focal points.
Separate the scalp and connecting tissues in the mediolateral axis, about 2.5–3 mm apart, using surgical tweezers and scissors or a mini retractor.
Clean and dry the surface of the exposed bone using triangle sponges and cotton swabs.

Determine Bregma and Lambda focal points by defining two points along an extrapolated straight line delineating the longitudinal sagittal suture, which intersects with an extrapolated continuous parabolic line delineating the anterior coronal suture (Bregma) and the posterior lambdoid suture (Lambda).
Attach the dental drill with its appropriate drill head to the stereotactic holder.
Mount the dental drill assembly to the stereotactic apparatus.
Align Bregma and Lambda in the horizontal plane using the binoculars.
Zero the position of the dental drill at Bregma on the z-axis.
Measure the position of the dental drill at Lambda.
Fine-tune the stereotactic apparatus to align Bregma and Lambda if necessary.
Determine the coordinates for cranial drilling: +0.4 mm ± 0.02 mm anterior-posterior axis, ±1.35 mm ± 0.02 mm mediolateral axis from Bregma.
Lower the dental drill slowly until it encounters soft brain tissue.
Stop drilling when transitioning from bone to soft brain tissue is observed.
Wash away remaining bone and blood with saline (0.9% NaCl).
Dry the area with swabs.
Replace the dental drill with a pipette holder.
Mount the glass pipette into the pipette holder.
Connect the pipette with a silicon tube to a 10 mL syringe.
Load 4.5 μL of the viral mixture onto a paraffin tape strip using a 1–10 μL pipette.
Bring the parafilm strip with the droplet under the fixed pipette.
Load the viral mixture into the pipette using negative pressure applied by the syringe.
Place the pipette filled with the viral mixture above the Bregma focal point.
Lower the pipette into the drill hole to a final depth of –6.39 ± 0.04 mm on the z-axis.
Inject 1–2 μL of the viral mixture per ganglion at a rate of about 1 μL per 10 s.
Visually monitor the viral mixture's fluid level during injection.
Perform the injection only when the fluid level in the pipette is higher than the margins of the drilled hole.
Maintain the injection pipette in place for a 5-minute pause time to allow pressure equalization.
After 5 min, lift out slowly the glass pipette and place it at the zero-reference point (Bregma).
Examine the pipette tip integrity.
Move the glass pipette to the second drill hole at the exact opposite coordinates in the x-axis for injecting the viral mixture into the second TG.
Wash and sponge the drill holes with saline 0.9%.
Dry the drill holes.
Suture the incision over the open dried and cleaned drill holes.
Apply synthomycine over the sutured incision.
Inject the mouse with atipamezole 150 μL IP.
Place the mouse in a cage under warming light and soothing conditions.
Monitor until the animal appears to recover (normal gait, grooming behavior, and overall appearance).
Move the mouse into a separate cage for 2–3 days to recover from the surgical procedure.
Place the mouse into a common cage with 2–4 littermates after recovery.
Perform a calibrating experiment on a separate group of mice to detect the optimal expression of RFP tracer using an epifluorescent microscope in anesthetized mice.
Monitor RFP fluorescence in corneal nerve terminals every day following viral injection for 10-14 days.
Optimal expression of RFP and GCaMP6s signals is achieved at 10–14 days post-viral injection.
Inject the mouse IP with 220–250 μL of the anesthesia mixture.
Hydrate both eyes by applying approximately 10 μL SES per eye.
Reapply SES to the non-imaged eye if it slips or vaporizes during the experiment.
Place the mouse on a heating pad set to 37°C located on a recording plate.
Stabilize the mouse's head with a three-point head stabilizer.
Tilt the head such that the imaged eye is in the horizontal plane.
Place the eye stabilizer over the mouse eye.
Gently stretch the skin around the eyeball aside using two fingers to bulge out the eyeball.
Carefully push the bulged eyeball through the hole of the eye stabilizer and bath.
Inspect to ensure that the eye stabilizer and bath is parallel to the horizontal plane.
Lift the eye stabilizer gently and readjust it if necessary.
Fill the eye stabilizer and bath with SES.
Inspect to ensure there is no tilt of the chamber in relation to the horizontal plane.
Remove the solution and readjust if it does not fill the eyecup homogeneously around the eyeball.
Place the plate with the mouse on the microscope stage.
Use an Exi Aqua (QImaging) monochromatic camera for wide-field epifluorescence image acquisition.
Acquire bright field imaging.
Acquire RFP fluorescence.
Center the cornea.
Adjust the field of view via the eye-piece using the 5X objective.
Use a 40× water immersion high NA objective and RFP filter set for imaging.
Select a superficial terminal with an exposure time of 300–500 ms, binning of 2 × 2, and hardware gain of 10–20.
Prepare the glass pipette as detailed in preparations for in vivo optical recording of calcium signals.
Fill the prepared glass pipette with the solution containing SES, capsaicin (500 nM), and SR101 (9 μM).
Discard trapped air bubbles at the tip of the puff pipette by gently flicking.
Place the filled puff pipette into the Picospritzer holder attached to the adapter on the micromanipulator.
Lift the 40× objective several hundreds of μm above the epithelial plane without changing its x and y coordinates.
Replace the 40× objective with a 5× objective.
Bring the pipette tip above the bath solution to the objective focal plane using an external light source.
Adjust the pipette tip to the center of the imaged field.
Place the 40× objective back in position.
Readjust the focal plane to bring the pipette tip into focus and to the center of the field of view.
Switch the optical pathway from the eye-piece to the QImaging camera.
Set parameters for RFP fluorescence acquisition.
Perform a short test puff to ensure the pipette is not blocked or leaking.
Monitor the change in SR101 fluorescence around the pipette tip after applying a puff using RFP fluorescence acquisition parameters.
Position the loaded pipette in close proximity to the terminal of interest using a micromanipulator.
Gradually lower the objective (40×) and the pipette consecutively, starting with increments of 20–40 μm.
Narrow the range when reaching closer to the terminal tip plane.
Repeat this process until the pipette tip is placed 2–5 μm above the corneal surface without disturbing the cell layer.
Place the pipette approximately 10 μm in the x-y plane from the terminal end.
Change the optical pathway so that the fluorescent emission is directed towards the RedShirt camera (back-illuminated 80 × 80 pixels cooled and fast CCD camera).
Set the RedShirt camera detection parameters to an acquisition rate of 40–125 Hz, medium gain, and “live view” mode.
Re-focus the microscope and bring the terminal to the center of the frame.
Set GFP fluorescence parameters (a 490 nm excitation LED and GFP filter (Ex 480, Em 535, dichroic Lp 510; Chroma)).
Choose regions of interest within 5–10 μm proximal to the terminal tip for detecting calcium-mediated changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence at terminals.
Choose regions of interest within 15–30 μm proximal to the terminal tip for detecting calcium-mediated changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence at fibers.
Choose regions of interest (ROIs) within 60–100 μm proximal to the terminal tip.
Apply capsaicin above the terminal tip.
Visualize ROI using recording software (Turbo-SM).
Trigger puff and start recording changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence via Turbo-SM.
Trigger Digidata 1440 A/D interface through Turbo-SM’s RedShirt camera analog-to-digital converter.
Initiate puff using Picospritzer triggered by Digidata 1440 A/D interface.
Set experimental parameters using pClamp software.
Calibrate the dispersion profile of puffed substances using sulfa-rhodamine 101 (SR101, 9 μM).
Measure changes in fluorescence intensity profile with distance from the pipette tip.
Use a pipette with 4–6 MΩ resistance filled with SES for puff application.
Connect the pipette to a picospritzer for capsaicin or vehicle application.
Apply puffs with a duration of 1 second at 2 pounds per square inch (psi).
Calibrate puff characteristics to achieve a substantial decrease in fluorescence at 15 μm from the pipette tip on the horizontal plane.
Place the pipette about 10 μm from the terminal tip for subsequent experiments.
Ensure the concentration of capsaicin at the terminal is close to the half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of TRPV1 channels (∼150 nM).
Record calcium-induced signals at designated ROIs using Turbo-SM imaging software following terminal activation.
Ensure the puff pipette does not touch the corneal surface during use.
Replace the puff pipette if it touches the corneal surface and use a new terminal located at least 100 μm away from the initial site.
Mark the puff pipette location before initiating each puff application.
Return the puff pipette to its original marked location after each puff application.
Fill two pulled glass pipettes (tip diameter ∼10 μm, ∼50KΩ) with SES.
Thread an Ag/AgCl electrode into each filled pipette.
Connect electrodes to an Iso-flex battery pack and controller.
Command the stimulation setup using a Digidata 1440 A/D interface.
Add a known resistor to the circuit for measuring the stimulation current.
Measure potential across the added resistor with an oscilloscope.
Place stimulating pipettes slightly above the corneal surface without disturbing the cell layer.
Position each stimulating pipette on opposing sides of a designated terminal, approximately 5-10 μm from the activated terminals.
Apply a series of current stimuli to determine the "rheobase" stimulus for each terminal.
